claim: Microglia are necessary for the normal functional development of adult-born granule cells (abGCs) in the olfactory bulb.
source: By transiently depleting microglia from the healthy adult mouse brain, we show that microglia are necessary for the normal functional development of adult-born granule cells (abGCs) in the olfactory bulb.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced odor responses in abGCs when microglia are depleted during development (Figures 2-3).

claim: Microglial depletion reduces the odor responses of developing, but not preexisting GCs in vivo in both awake and anesthetized mice.
source: Microglial depletion reduces the odor responses of developing, but not preexisting GCs in vivo in both awake and anesthetized mice.
evidence: Supported by in vivo calcium imaging data showing reduced responses in developing abGCs (Figures 2-3) but not in mature abGCs (Figure 4).

claim: Microglia preferentially target their motile processes to interact with mushroom spines on abGCs.
source: Microglia preferentially target their motile processes to interact with mushroom spines on abGCs, and when microglia are absent, abGCs develop smaller spines and receive weaker excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging showing microglia interact more frequently with mushroom spines than predicted by chance (Figure 1E).

claim: When microglia are absent, abGCs develop smaller spines.
source: Microglia preferentially target their motile processes to interact with mushroom spines on abGCs, and when microglia are absent, abGCs develop smaller spines and receive weaker excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data showing reduced spine head volumes in PLX-treated mice (Figure 5D).

claim: When microglia are absent, abGCs receive weaker excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: Microglia preferentially target their motile processes to interact with mushroom spines on abGCs, and when microglia are absent, abGCs develop smaller spines and receive weaker excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data showing reduced sEPSC amplitude in PLX-treated mice (Figure 6D).

claim: Microglia promote the development of excitatory synapses onto developing abGCs.
source: These results suggest that microglia promote the development of excitatory synapses onto developing abGCs, which may impact the function of these cells in the olfactory circuit.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced spine size and weaker excitatory inputs in the absence of microglia.

claim: Microglia are critically important for normal brain development in the embryonic and early postnatal stages.
source: Microglia are critically important for normal brain development in the embryonic and early postnatal stages (Hammond et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hammond et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia have been implicated in diverse neurodevelopmental functions.
source: Originally thought to be primarily involved in injury and disease, many recent studies have implicated microglia in diverse neurodevelopmental functions (Tremblay et al., 2011; Salter and Beggs, 2014; Wu et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Much less is known about what role microglia might play in the healthy adult brain.
source: However, much less is known about what role microglia might play in the healthy adult brain, even during the process of adult neurogenesis, which can be thought of as an extension of developmental processes throughout the lifespan.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature indicating a knowledge gap.

claim: Microglia have been implicated in activity-dependent synaptic pruning during early postnatal development.
source: During early postnatal development, microglia have been implicated in the regulation of synaptic development, including activity-dependent synaptic pruning (Stevens et al., 2007; Schafer et al., 2012; Tremblay et al., 2010; Paolicelli et al., 2011; Gunner et al., 2019) on one hand and promotion of synaptic development and maturation on the other (Hoshiko et al., 2012; Zhan et al., 2014; Miyamoto et al., 2016; Nakayama et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Microglia have been implicated in promotion of synaptic development and maturation during early postnatal development.
source: During early postnatal development, microglia have been implicated in the regulation of synaptic development, including activity-dependent synaptic pruning (Stevens et al., 2007; Schafer et al., 2012; Tremblay et al., 2010; Paolicelli et al., 2011; Gunner et al., 2019) on one hand and promotion of synaptic development and maturation on the other (Hoshiko et al., 2012; Zhan et al., 2014; Miyamoto et al., 2016; Nakayama et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal adult neurogenesis is impaired in models of neuroinflammation.
source: For example, hippocampal adult neurogenesis is impaired in models of neuroinflammation (Monje et al., 2003; Ekdahl et al., 2003) and in immune-deficient mice (Ziv et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Monje et al., 2003 and Ekdahl et al., 2003.

claim: Hippocampal adult neurogenesis is impaired in immune-deficient mice.
source: For example, hippocampal adult neurogenesis is impaired in models of neuroinflammation (Monje et al., 2003; Ekdahl et al., 2003) and in immune-deficient mice (Ziv et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ziv et al., 2006.

claim: Microglia regulate adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the DG through ongoing phagocytosis of apoptotic neuroblasts.
source: Microglia regulate adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the DG through ongoing phagocytosis of apoptotic neuroblasts (Sierra et al., 2010), although they do not seem to be similarly involved in the subventricular zone (SVZ) or rostral migratory stream (RMS) (Kyle et al., 2019; but see Ribeiro Xavier et al., 2015 for counterevidence).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sierra et al., 2010.

claim: Microglia do not seem to be similarly involved in the subventricular zone (SVZ) or rostral migratory stream (RMS).
source: Microglia regulate adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the DG through ongoing phagocytosis of apoptotic neuroblasts (Sierra et al., 2010), although they do not seem to be similarly involved in the subventricular zone (SVZ) or rostral migratory stream (RMS) (Kyle et al., 2019; but see Ribeiro Xavier et al., 2015 for counterevidence).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kyle et al., 2019, with counterevidence noted from Ribeiro Xavier et al., 2015.

claim: Microglial activation via sensory deafferentation in the OB decreases the number of adult-born neurons.
source: Microglial activation via sensory deafferentation in the OB decreases the number of adult-born neurons (Lazarini et al., 2012) and their spine density (Denizet et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lazarini et al., 2012.

claim: Microglial activation via sensory deafferentation in the OB decreases spine density of adult-born neurons.
source: Microglial activation via sensory deafferentation in the OB decreases the number of adult-born neurons (Lazarini et al., 2012) and their spine density (Denizet et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Denizet et al., 2017.

claim: Lipopolysaccharide injection or CX3CR1 knockout activates microglia in the hippocampus and alters both inhibitory and excitatory synapses onto adult-born neurons in the DG.
source: In addition, lipopolysaccharide injection or CX3CR1 knockout activates microglia in the hippocampus and alters both inhibitory (Jakubs et al., 2008) and excitatory (Bolós et al., 2018) synapses onto adult-born neurons in the DG.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jakubs et al., 2008 and Bolós et al., 2018.

claim: A recent study documented increased activity in principal neurons in the OB after microglial depletion.
source: A recent study documented increased activity in principal neurons in the OB after microglial depletion (Reshef et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reshef et al., 2017.

claim: Microglial processes were highly motile and occasionally appeared in close proximity to labeled dendritic spines.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005; Tremblay et al., 2010), we found that microglial processes were highly motile and occasionally appeared in close proximity to labeled dendritic spines (Video 2, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data (Video 2, Figure 1B) and consistent with previous literature (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005; Tremblay et al., 2010).

claim: Microglia interacted with 38.5% of abGC dendritic spines classified as 'mushroom' spines during 30-90 min imaging sessions.
source: Microglia exhibited an impressive degree of motility, interacting with 38.5% of abGC dendritic spines classified as 'mushroom' spines (Figure 1C) and 27.2% of spines classified as 'filopodial' spines (Figure 1H) during the course of our 30–90 min imaging sessions, which was not significantly different from the offset data (p=0.13 and p=0.39, respectively) (Figure 1D,I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data (Figure 1C, 1D).

claim: Microglia interacted with 27.2% of spines classified as 'filopodial' spines during 30-90 min imaging sessions.
source: Microglia exhibited an impressive degree of motility, interacting with 38.5% of abGC dendritic spines classified as 'mushroom' spines (Figure 1C) and 27.2% of spines classified as 'filopodial' spines (Figure 1H) during the course of our 30–90 min imaging sessions, which was not significantly different from the offset data (p=0.13 and p=0.39, respectively) (Figure 1D,I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data (Figure 1H, 1I).

claim: Microglia interacted significantly more often with individual mushroom spines than predicted by chance.
source: However, we found that microglia interacted significantly more often with individual mushroom spines than predicted by chance (Data: mean 0.15 ± 0.00039 interactions/10 min vs. Offsets: mean 0.12 ± 0.016 interactions/10 min, p=0.048) (Figure 1E) though the length of individual interactions was not significantly greater(p=0.96) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of real data to offset controls (Figure 1E).

claim: The length of individual interactions between microglia and mushroom spines was not significantly greater than predicted by chance.
source: However, we found that microglia interacted significantly more often with individual mushroom spines than predicted by chance (Data: mean 0.15 ± 0.00039 interactions/10 min vs. Offsets: mean 0.12 ± 0.016 interactions/10 min, p=0.048) (Figure 1E) though the length of individual interactions was not significantly greater(p=0.96) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison showing no significant difference (Figure 1F).

claim: Microglia did not interact with filopodial spines at levels above chance.
source: In contrast, microglia did not interact with filopodial spines at levels above chance (Figure 1I–L).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference from offset controls (Figure 1I-L).

claim: Microglia specifically interact with spines that likely contain functional synapses.
source: These results suggest that microglia specifically interact with spines that likely contain functional synapses (Whitman and Greer, 2007), positioning them to influence synaptic stabilization and maturation during the early development of abGCs.
evidence: Inferred from the preferential interaction with mushroom spines, which are known to contain functional synapses (Whitman and Greer, 2007).

claim: Microglial depletion using PLX5622 efficiently ablated microglia from the OB (85% ablation as assessed by immunostaining, 96% ablation as assessed by flow cytometry) within one week.
source: Microglial depletion using the CSF1R inhibitor PLX5622 (hereafter PLX) formulated in chow as previously described (Elmore et al., 2014) efficiently ablated microglia from the OB (85% ablation as assessed by immunostaining, 96% ablation as assessed by flow cytometry) within one week and depletion could be maintained at similar levels for up to nine weeks with ongoing delivery (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and flow cytometry data (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).

claim: Microglial depletion could be maintained at similar levels for up to nine weeks with ongoing delivery of PLX5622.
source: Microglial depletion using the CSF1R inhibitor PLX5622 (hereafter PLX) formulated in chow as previously described (Elmore et al., 2014) efficiently ablated microglia from the OB (85% ablation as assessed by immunostaining, 96% ablation as assessed by flow cytometry) within one week and depletion could be maintained at similar levels for up to nine weeks with ongoing delivery (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal immunostaining data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: There was no evidence of any largescale inflammatory response to microglial depletion, as assessed by immunostaining of GFAP.
source: We found no evidence of any largescale inflammatory response to microglial depletion, as assessed by immunostaining of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), consistent with previous reports of the effects of PLX on the whole brain (Elmore et al., 2014) and the olfactory bulb (Reshef et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by GFAP immunostaining data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and consistent with previous reports (Elmore et al., 2014; Reshef et al., 2017).

claim: The distribution of responses was shifted left toward lower responsiveness in PLX-treated mice.
source: The distribution was shifted left toward lower responsiveness in PLX-treated mice (p=2.56e-08) while the noise distributions constructed from blank trials were not different (p=0.96) (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data (Figure 2F).

claim: Dendrites in PLX-treated mice responded to fewer odors than control mice.
source: Dendrites in PLX-treated mice also responded to fewer odors (for threshold response criteria, see Materials and methods, In vivo imaging analysis, Thresholds) (median (IQR): Control: 3 (1–6), PLX: 1 (0–4), p=1.16e-04) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of odor responses (Figure 2G).

claim: Lifetime sparseness was lower in dendrites in PLX-treated mice.
source: We also found that lifetime sparseness (Willmore and Tolhurst, 2001), (bounded between 0 and 1, a low score indicates a sparser representation) was lower in dendrites in PLX-treated mice (median (IQR): Control: 0.18 (0.067–0.32), PLX: 0.067 (0–0.25), p=4.18e-04) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of odor responses (Figure 2H).

claim: There was no difference in the median amplitude of responses above threshold between control and PLX-treated mice.
source: However, there was no difference in the median amplitude of responses above threshold (p=0.77) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5F), suggesting that the difference in overall responses was mostly mediated by an increase in the proportion of dendrites that did not respond to any of the odors in our panel, which was significantly higher in PLX-treated mice (Control: 0.14 ± 0.039, PLX: 0.32 ± 0.039, p=0.0013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical bootstrap analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 5F).

claim: The proportion of dendrites that did not respond to any odors was significantly higher in PLX-treated mice.
source: However, there was no difference in the median amplitude of responses above threshold (p=0.77) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5F), suggesting that the difference in overall responses was mostly mediated by an increase in the proportion of dendrites that did not respond to any of the odors in our panel, which was significantly higher in PLX-treated mice (Control: 0.14 ± 0.039, PLX: 0.32 ± 0.039, p=0.0013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical bootstrap analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).

claim: Granule cell odor representation is significantly different in awake mice compared to anesthetized mice.
source: While imaging in anesthetized mice allows better control of breathing rate, brain motion, and possible motivational influences on brain state, granule cell odor representation is significantly different in awake mice (Kato et al., 2012; Wienisch and Murthy, 2016; Wallace et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kato et al., 2012; Wienisch and Murthy, 2016; Wallace et al., 2017).

claim: In awake mice, dendrites in PLX-treated mice had lower responsiveness than control mice.
source: Therefore, we also imaged abGC dendrites in awake mice and found similar effects as in anesthetized mice (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Dendrites in PLX-treated mice had lower responsiveness (p=0.037) (Figure 3B), responding to a lower median number of odors (median (IQR) Control: 1 (0–6), PLX: 0 (0–3), p=0.052) (Figure 3C) and having lower lifetime sparseness (median (IQR) Control: 0.067 (0–0.28), PLX: 0 (0–0.16), p=0.056) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in awake mice (Figure 3B).

claim: Response time courses were different between control and PLX-treated mice in the awake state.
source: Interestingly, while response time courses were similar between control and PLX-treated mice in the anesthetized state (p=0.30), allowing us to characterize responses with a simple mean across the odor analysis period, principal components analysis of the ΔF/Fσ traces for all cells' responses to all odors revealed different response time courses in awake mice (p=0.004) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by principal components analysis of calcium imaging data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Sniffing rates were not different between control and PLX-treated mice during baseline or odor presentation periods.
source: These differences were likely not due to changes in active sampling of odors since sniffing rates were not different during baseline or odor presentation periods (mean Baseline: Control = 3.49 Hz, PLX = 3.52 Hz, p=0.91; Odor: Control = 4.00 Hz, PLX = 3.94 Hz, p=0.81) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by breathing rate measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Microglial depletion after abGC development has no effect on the distribution of odor responses.
source: In this case, we found no significant differences in the distribution of responses (p=0.45) (Figure 4C), median number of odors evoking a significant response (median (IQR) Control: 1.5 (0–6), PLX: 2 (0–5), p=1.00) (Figure 4D), or lifetime sparseness (median (IQR) Control: 0.096 (0–0.31), PLX: 0.099 (0–0.27), p=0.86) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data before and after PLX treatment in mature abGCs (Figure 4C).

claim: Microglial depletion after abGC development has no effect on the median number of odors evoking a significant response.
source: In this case, we found no significant differences in the distribution of responses (p=0.45) (Figure 4C), median number of odors evoking a significant response (median (IQR) Control: 1.5 (0–6), PLX: 2 (0–5), p=1.00) (Figure 4D), or lifetime sparseness (median (IQR) Control: 0.096 (0–0.31), PLX: 0.099 (0–0.27), p=0.86) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data before and after PLX treatment in mature abGCs (Figure 4D).

claim: Microglial depletion after abGC development has no effect on lifetime sparseness.
source: In this case, we found no significant differences in the distribution of responses (p=0.45) (Figure 4C), median number of odors evoking a significant response (median (IQR) Control: 1.5 (0–6), PLX: 2 (0–5), p=1.00) (Figure 4D), or lifetime sparseness (median (IQR) Control: 0.096 (0–0.31), PLX: 0.099 (0–0.27), p=0.86) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data before and after PLX treatment in mature abGCs (Figure 4E).

claim: Even after 9 weeks of PLX treatment, the level of responsiveness remained stable in mature abGCs.
source: Even after 9 weeks of PLX treatment, the level of responsiveness remained stable in mature abGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data after extended PLX treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Spine density was higher in PLX-treated mice at 4 weeks post injection.
source: We found higher spine density (median (IQR): Control: 0.30 (0.21–0.36) spines/µm, PLX: 0.40 (0.31–0.48) spines/µm, p=0.039) (Figure 5C), but smaller spine head volumes in PLX-treated mice (mean Control: 0.37 ± 0.03 μm3, PLX: 0.31 ± 0.02 μm3, p=0.057) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of spine density (Figure 5C).

claim: Spine head volumes were smaller in PLX-treated mice at 4 weeks post injection.
source: We found higher spine density (median (IQR): Control: 0.30 (0.21–0.36) spines/µm, PLX: 0.40 (0.31–0.48) spines/µm, p=0.039) (Figure 5C), but smaller spine head volumes in PLX-treated mice (mean Control: 0.37 ± 0.03 μm3, PLX: 0.31 ± 0.02 μm3, p=0.057) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification of spine head volumes (Figure 5D).

claim: Most of the increase in spine density in PLX-treated mice was due to an increase in the density of filopodial spines.
source: Furthermore, most of the increase in spine density in PLX-treated mice was due to an increase in the density of filopodial spines that had similar spine head volumes as in control mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of spine subtypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Mushroom spines had significantly smaller head volumes in PLX-treated mice.
source: In contrast, mushroom spines had significantly smaller head volumes in PLX-treated mice (mean Control: 0.45 ± 0.04 μm3, PLX: 0.36 ± 0.03 μm3, p=0.036) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of mushroom spine volumes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The frequency of sEPSCs was similar in cells from control and PLX-treated mice.
source: We found a similar frequency of sEPSCs in cells from control and PLX-treated mice (mean Control: 30.8 ± 2.2 Hz, PLX: 30.6 ± 2.4 Hz, p=0.48) (Figure 6C), but their amplitude was reduced (mean Control: 10.8 ± 0.6 pA, PLX: 9.0 ± 0.4 pA, p=0.007) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 6C).

claim: The amplitude of sEPSCs was reduced in PLX-treated mice.
source: We found a similar frequency of sEPSCs in cells from control and PLX-treated mice (mean Control: 30.8 ± 2.2 Hz, PLX: 30.6 ± 2.4 Hz, p=0.48) (Figure 6C), but their amplitude was reduced (mean Control: 10.8 ± 0.6 pA, PLX: 9.0 ± 0.4 pA, p=0.007) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 6D).

claim: Passive membrane properties including membrane resistance and capacitance were unchanged in PLX-treated mice.
source: Passive membrane properties including membrane resistance (median Control: 597 MΩ, PLX: 532 MΩ, p=0.31) and capacitance (median Control: 14.2 pF, PLX: 13.6 pF, p=0.61) were unchanged, signifying no differences in cell surface area or resting membrane properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: There was no difference in the frequency or amplitude of sIPSCs between control and PLX-treated mice.
source: To check whether there might be accompanying changes in inhibition that could offset or augment the observed changes in excitation, we also recorded spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) in the same cells (Figure 6E). We found no difference in the frequency (p=0.77) (Figure 6F) or amplitude of sIPSCs (p=0.79) (Figure 6G), suggesting that abGCs that mature in the absence of microglia receive weaker excitatory inputs without noticeable accompanying changes in inhibition.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 6F, 6G).

claim: AbGCs that mature in the absence of microglia receive weaker excitatory inputs without noticeable accompanying changes in inhibition.
source: To check whether there might be accompanying changes in inhibition that could offset or augment the observed changes in excitation, we also recorded spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) in the same cells (Figure 6E). We found no difference in the frequency (p=0.77) (Figure 6F) or amplitude of sIPSCs (p=0.79) (Figure 6G), suggesting that abGCs that mature in the absence of microglia receive weaker excitatory inputs without noticeable accompanying changes in inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of reduced excitatory inputs and unchanged inhibitory inputs.

claim: There was no significant change in the frequency of sEPSCs in abGCs that experienced three weeks of microglial depletion after three months of maturation.
source: There was no significant change in the frequency (p=0.76) (Figure 7B) or amplitude of sEPSCs (p=0.09) (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings in mature abGCs (Figure 7B).

claim: There was no significant change in the amplitude of sEPSCs in abGCs that experienced three weeks of microglial depletion after three months of maturation.
source: There was no significant change in the frequency (p=0.76) (Figure 7B) or amplitude of sEPSCs (p=0.09) (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings in mature abGCs (Figure 7C).

claim: Microglial depletion only affects synaptic inputs to abGCs when it occurs during the first five to six weeks of the cells' development rather than after maturation.
source: These results suggest that microglial depletion only affects synaptic inputs to abGCs when it occurs during the first five to six weeks of the cells' development rather than after maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of effects during development (Figure 6) versus after maturation (Figure 7).

claim: This study is the first to link microglial depletion directly to changes in the in vivo activity and functional inputs of a specific affected cell population.
source: Importantly, our study is the first to link microglial depletion directly to changes in the in vivo activity and functional inputs of a specific affected cell population.
evidence: Based on comparison with existing literature and the novelty of the combined approach.

claim: The dampened responses observed in abGCs are consistent with reduced spine volume and weaker excitatory inputs in neurons that develop in the absence of microglia.
source: Furthermore, we go on to investigate the physiological mechanisms and show that the dampened responses we observe are consistent with reduced spine volume and weaker excitatory inputs in neurons that develop in the absence of microglia.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of reduced odor responses, smaller spines, and weaker excitatory inputs.

claim: Inflammation in the OB has been shown to generally reduce adult-born neuron numbers and spine density.
source: However, inflammation in the OB has been shown to generally reduce adult-born neuron numbers (Lazarini et al., 2012) and spine density (Denizet et al., 2017) as opposed to increasing spine density and reducing excitatory synapse strength as we show here, so it is unlikely that undetected inflammation relating to microglial depletion can fully account for the results we observe.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lazarini et al., 2012 and Denizet et al., 2017.

claim: It is unlikely that undetected inflammation relating to microglial depletion can fully account for the results observed.
source: However, inflammation in the OB has been shown to generally reduce adult-born neuron numbers (Lazarini et al., 2012) and spine density (Denizet et al., 2017) as opposed to increasing spine density and reducing excitatory synapse strength as we show here, so it is unlikely that undetected inflammation relating to microglial depletion can fully account for the results we observe.
evidence: Inferred from the opposite effects of inflammation compared to the observed results.

claim: AbGCs receive local inputs from within the OB as well as feedback from other cortical areas and neuromodulatory inputs.
source: AbGCs receive local inputs from within the OB as well as feedback from other cortical areas and neuromodulatory inputs (Lepousez et al., 2013), so we cannot unambiguously attribute the effects on abGCs to changes within the OB.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lepousez et al., 2013.

claim: The effects on abGCs cannot be unambiguously attributed to changes within the OB due to brain-wide microglial depletion.
source: AbGCs receive local inputs from within the OB as well as feedback from other cortical areas and neuromodulatory inputs (Lepousez et al., 2013), so we cannot unambiguously attribute the effects on abGCs to changes within the OB.
evidence: Inferred from the brain-wide nature of PLX5622 treatment and the diverse inputs to abGCs.

claim: AbGCs become responsive to odor stimuli soon after they arrive in the OB and then undergo a period of functional refinement during which their initially broadly tuned responses become more selective.
source: AbGCs become responsive to odor stimuli soon after they arrive in the OB and then undergo a period of functional refinement during which their initially broadly tuned responses become more selective (Wallace et al., 2017) (although there may also be a subpopulation of abGCs that shows broadening of responses with maturation Quast et al., 2017; Wallace et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wallace et al., 2017 and Quast et al., 2017.

claim: The mechanism behind the increase in stimulus selectivity in abGCs may involve both a decrease in some aspects of excitability and selective reorganization of synaptic inputs.
source: Although the mechanism behind this increase in stimulus selectivity is not well-understood, it may involve both a decrease in some aspects of excitability (Carleton et al., 2003; Nissant et al., 2009), especially dendritic excitability (Wallace et al., 2017), as well as selective reorganization of synaptic inputs such that mature abGCs become more responsive to a particular glomerular module at the expense of other inputs.
evidence: Based on citations to previous studies (Carleton et al., 2003; Nissant et al., 2009; Wallace et al., 2017) and speculation about mechanisms.

claim: AbGCs in PLX-treated mice experience a normal drop in excitability without a concomitant selective strengthening of specific synaptic inputs, leading to sparser odor responses.
source: We propose that abGCs in PLX-treated mice experience a normal drop in excitability (likely regulated by cell-intrinsic mechanisms) without a concomitant selective strengthening of specific synaptic inputs, leading to sparser odor responses (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed data and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The higher density of more filopodial-like spines in PLX-treated mice is characteristic of abGCs at an earlier stage of maturation.
source: This is consistent with the higher density of more filopodial-like spines in PLX-treated mice (characteristic of abGCs at an earlier stage of maturation Breton-Provencher et al., 2014) along with smaller mushroom spines (Figure 5) and lower amplitude sEPSCs (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by citation to Breton-Provencher et al., 2014.

claim: Excitability has been mainly shown to affect survival rather than synaptic inputs in abGCs.
source: It is also possible that abGCs in PLX-treated mice could have generally lower excitability, but we regard this as unlikely since excitability has been mainly shown to affect survival rather than synaptic inputs in abGCs (Lin et al., 2010), in contrast to what we observe here.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2010.

claim: The effects on synaptic development observed in individual cells are modest (~15% reduction in median sEPSC amplitude in PLX-treated mice).
source: Though the effects on synaptic development that we observe in individual cells are modest (~15% reduction in median sEPSC amplitude in PLX-treated mice, Figure 6C), these effects combined nonlinearly across many synapses likely become important near response threshold in vivo.
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of electrophysiology data (Figure 6C).

claim: Modest effects on individual synapses combined nonlinearly across many synapses likely become important near response threshold in vivo.
source: Though the effects on synaptic development that we observe in individual cells are modest (~15% reduction in median sEPSC amplitude in PLX-treated mice, Figure 6C), these effects combined nonlinearly across many synapses likely become important near response threshold in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference about how small synaptic changes could lead to larger functional effects.

claim: Calcium responses recorded in vivo likely represent dendritic calcium spikes or global calcium events accompanying somatic action potentials that result from simultaneous activation of many feedforward and feedback synapses.
source: Indeed, we observed larger effects on calcium responses recorded in vivo (median response amplitudes halved across all abGCs imaged in each PLX-treated animal, Figure 2—figure supplement 5D), which likely represent dendritic calcium spikes or global calcium events accompanying somatic action potentials that result from simultaneous activation of many feedforward and feedback synapses (Egger et al., 2005; Egger, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Egger et al., 2005 and Egger, 2008.

claim: It has been unclear whether microglia interact with synapses more often than would be expected by chance, given the dense synaptic milieu of the adult brain and the high degree of microglial process motility.
source: Though several studies have examined microglial motility (Nimmerjahn et al., 2005) and interactions between microglia and neuronal elements (Wake et al., 2009; Tremblay et al., 2010; Sipe et al., 2016), it has been unclear whether microglia interact with synapses more often than would be expected by chance, given the dense synaptic milieu of the adult brain and the high degree of microglial process motility.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature and identification of a knowledge gap.

claim: Automated methods were used to segment microglial processes from in vivo two-photon time-lapse imaging experiments and shuffle the resulting images for comparison.
source: Using automated methods to segment microglial processes from in vivo two-photon time-lapse imaging experiments and shuffle the resulting images for comparison, we demonstrated targeted motility towards mushroom spines on abGCs, which are likely to contain established excitatory synapses (Whitman and Greer, 2007).
evidence: Description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: In the absence of microglia, fewer spines attain mushroom morphology, leading to overall reduced spine volume and correspondingly weaker excitatory synapses.
source: In the absence of microglia, we suggest that fewer spines attain mushroom morphology, leading to overall reduced spine volume and correspondingly weaker excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the observed data.

claim: An increase in spine density in microglia-ablated animals is likely accounted for by filopodial spines which did not have functional or stable synapses.
source: Concomitantly, we observed an increase in spine density in microglia-ablated animals, which is likely accounted for by filopodial spines which did not have functional or stable synapses (since we did not see an accompanying increase in the frequency of synaptic currents in PLX-treated mice).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased spine density without increased sEPSC frequency.

claim: One potential unifying hypothesis is that microglia may prune weaker synapses, allowing stronger synapses to strengthen further.
source: One potential unifying hypothesis is that microglia may prune weaker synapses, allowing stronger synapses to strengthen further (Stevens et al., 2007; Schafer et al., 2012; Tremblay et al., 2010; Paolicelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Unlike other sensory systems that experience largescale pruning events during development, abGCs develop an increasing number of synapses over time.
source: However, unlike other sensory systems that experience largescale pruning events during development, abGCs develop an increasing number of synapses over time (Carleton et al., 2003; Breton-Provencher et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carleton et al., 2003 and Breton-Provencher et al., 2014.

claim: It remains possible that microglia could prune presynaptic elements or that the frame rate was too slow to observe pruning events.
source: Although we did not directly observe pruning of dendritic spines in abGCs in our time lapse imaging experiments, it remains possible that microglia could prune presynaptic elements (Schafer et al., 2012; Gunner et al., 2019)(which we did not image) or that our frame rate was too slow to observe such events (Weinhard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation about limitations of the imaging approach, supported by citations.

claim: Deficits in microglial CX3CR1 have been linked to weaker synapses and impaired connectivity.
source: In addition to synaptic pruning, microglia may be involved in promoting synaptic strengthening. Deficits in microglial CX3CR1 have been linked to weaker synapses and impaired connectivity (Zhan et al., 2014; Reshef et al., 2017) as well as delays in maturation of the AMPA/NMDA ratio (Hoshiko et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhan et al., 2014 and Reshef et al., 2017.

claim: Deficits in microglial CX3CR1 have been linked to delays in maturation of the AMPA/NMDA ratio.
source: In addition to synaptic pruning, microglia may be involved in promoting synaptic strengthening. Deficits in microglial CX3CR1 have been linked to weaker synapses and impaired connectivity (Zhan et al., 2014; Reshef et al., 2017) as well as delays in maturation of the AMPA/NMDA ratio (Hoshiko et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoshiko et al., 2012.

claim: It is still unclear whether the effects of CX3CR1 deficits are related to differences in spine surveillance and direct microglial-neuron signaling or due to altered microglial behavior.
source: It is still unclear whether these effects, similar to those that we observe in the PLX ablation model, are related to differences in spine surveillance and direct microglial-neuron signaling or due to altered microglial behavior, including changes in release of moderating factors or interactions with other cell types, such as astrocytes.
evidence: This identifies an open question about mechanisms.

claim: Microglia may also regulate neuronal excitability through mechanisms other than synaptic regulation.
source: In addition, although most previous work has focused on microglial regulation of synapses, microglia may also regulate neuronal excitability through other mechanisms (Li et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2012 and Peng et al., 2019.

claim: The study cannot exclude additional possible effects of microglia on nonsynaptic aspects of abGC development.
source: Accordingly, although we found no differences in passive membrane properties between abGCs in control versus PLX-treated animals, we cannot exclude additional possible effects of microglia on nonsynaptic aspects of abGC development, including active dendritic properties, that could also contribute to the reduced responsiveness we observe when microglia are ablated.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the study.

claim: The effect of microglial depletion is specific to developing abGCs.
source: While our results suggest that the effect of microglial depletion is specific to developing abGCs (since our results with microglial depletion after abGC development did not reach statistical significance in most cases), we saw similar trends in reduced responses and excitatory inputs regardless of the timing of microglial depletion.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of effects during versus after development.

claim: Lentiviral labeling is an imperfect method for isolating a single cohort of abGCs.
source: This could be because lentiviral labeling is an imperfect method for isolating a single cohort of abGCs (so some abGCs in the 'after development group' may still be at an earlier stage of development – see discussion of newcomer cells in Wallace et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration supported by citation to Wallace et al., 2017.

claim: Microglial depletion may also affect mature abGCs, although to a lesser extent than developing abGCs.
source: Another possibility is that microglial depletion also affects mature abGCs, although to a lesser extent than developing abGCs.
evidence: This is speculation about possible effects on mature cells.

claim: Microglia may be involved in the general maturation or strengthening of newly formed excitatory synapses in GCs.
source: This could be because microglia may be involved in the general maturation or strengthening of newly formed excitatory synapses in GCs, and even mature GCs have high rates of synapse formation (and elimination) compared to cells in other brain regions (Mizrahi, 2007; Sailor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Mizrahi, 2007 and Sailor et al., 2016.

claim: Mature GCs have high rates of synapse formation and elimination compared to cells in other brain regions.
source: This could be because microglia may be involved in the general maturation or strengthening of newly formed excitatory synapses in GCs, and even mature GCs have high rates of synapse formation (and elimination) compared to cells in other brain regions (Mizrahi, 2007; Sailor et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mizrahi, 2007 and Sailor et al., 2016.

claim: The larger effect of microglial depletion on developing rather than mature adult-born neurons highlights the role of microglia during developmental stages.
source: The larger effect of microglial depletion on developing rather than mature adult-born neurons highlights the role of microglia during developmental stages and may explain why some studies have not found significant effects of microglial depletion in other areas of the healthy adult brain (Elmore et al., 2014; Torres et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: The reduced activity observed in mature abGCs after microglial depletion is consistent with increased activity in the principal cells they inhibit.
source: The reduced activity that we observe in mature abGCs after microglial depletion is consistent with increased activity in the principal cells they inhibit (Reshef et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous work, supported by citation to Reshef et al., 2017.

claim: Reduced inhibition from GCs to OB principal neurons has been directly linked to an increase in the time needed to discriminate odors in challenging olfactory tasks.
source: Since reduced inhibition from GCs to OB principal neurons has been directly linked to an increase in the time needed to discriminate odors in challenging olfactory tasks (Abraham et al., 2010), this alteration in the OB circuitry could have functional consequences (Egger and Urban, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abraham et al., 2010 and Egger and Urban, 2006.

claim: AbGCs may have an outsized role in the plasticity that underlies complex olfactory behaviors.
source: Furthermore, given that abGCs may have an outsized role in the plasticity that underlies complex olfactory behaviors (Breton-Provencher et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2000; Mandairon et al., 2018), microglial regulation of their development may contribute to ongoing plasticity in the olfactory system.
evidence: Supported by citations to Breton-Provencher et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2000; and Mandairon et al., 2018.

claim: Microglial regulation of abGC development may contribute to ongoing plasticity in the olfactory system.
source: Furthermore, given that abGCs may have an outsized role in the plasticity that underlies complex olfactory behaviors (Breton-Provencher et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2000; Mandairon et al., 2018), microglial regulation of their development may contribute to ongoing plasticity in the olfactory system.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Microglial depletion did not affect the overall number of adult-born neurons in the OB.
source: Microglial depletion did not affect the overall number of adult-born neurons in the OB (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), consistent with other reports, (Reshef et al., 2017; Kyle et al., 2019), and we could readily identify dTomato-labeled abGC dendrites in control and PLX-treated mice.
evidence: Supported by BrdU quantification data (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and consistent with previous reports.

claim: GCs in the OB are axonless and their release sites are located at dendodendritic synapses on spines in the EPL.
source: Since GCs in the OB are axonless and their release sites are located at dendodendritic synapses on spines in the EPL (Rall et al., 1966), we chose to record calcium responses in these dendrites.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rall et al., 1966.
